title: Canadian military will keep firing howitzers to trigger B.C. avalanches, pausing plan to end program | CBC News
html:
British Columbia

Canadian military will keep firing howitzers to trigger B.C. avalanches, pausing plan to end program

Operation Palaci is the longest running Forces operation in Canadian history, according to Parks Canada

The sound of howitzers will continue to be heard in the B.C. mountains.

Parks Canada and the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) say that after "further consideration," they no longer have plans to end Operation Palaci, a long-running avalanche control program in Rogers Pass through the Selkirk Mountains in Glacier National Park.

For more than 70 years, CAF personnel have been firing large howitzers at the mountains that line the Trans-Canada Highway between Revelstoke and Golden, B.C., in order to trigger small, controlled snow slides that can be easily cleared from the highway and railway and avoid larger, hazardous avalanches.

But that program was scheduled to come to an end after this season, with the program formally expiring in August 2027.

At the time, the Department of National Defence (DND) said the change was due to evolving defence and military priorities.

However, in a statement released Thursday and confirmed by the CAF, Parks Canada said the program will be continuing indefinitely.

"Public safety in Rogers Pass remains a priority for the Government of Canada," the statement says.

"The reliability of this section of the Trans-Canada Highway is critical to the Canadian economy. Following further consideration, there is currently no set date for the end of Operation Palaci."

It goes on to say to the two organizations are "working together to develop a transition plan regarding the future of avalanche control" but the CAF "will continue to support avalanche control until further notice."

Neither agency specified why the decision to end the program next year had been reversed.

About the program

The 43-kilometre stretch of mountainous highway where Operation Palaci takes place poses unique challenges due to its high elevation, and high density of avalanche slopes.

Historically, these features made the howitzers the most efficient method of avalanche management.

It is the longest running Canadian Armed Forces operation in the country's history, according to Parks Canada.

A 105-millimetre howitzer in position at Rogers Pass, B.C. on Wednesday, March 4, 2015. (Jeff Bassett/The Canadian Press)

It is also the only avalanche program currently managed by the DND, and is also the world’s largest mobile avalanche control program.

The operation manages avalanche hazards from 16 gun positions that mark 135 avalanche paths and approximately 270 artillery targets, according to Parks Canada.
summary: Parks Canada and the Canadian Armed Forces say that after "further consideration," they no longer have plans to end Operation Palaci, a long-running avalanche control program in Rogers Pass through the Selkirk Mountains in Glacier National Park.
